# Resumable Text Editor Search: Hand-Written vs Generated State Machines on PicoCalc P4

## 1. Scope

This report examines whether compiler-generated cooperative yield machinery can replace hand-written continuation state machines in a text editor running as a Wasm or RV32 guest on the PicoCalc P4. The manual arm is pre-G revision `1357545`, which uses hand-written continuations and E language tasks E1–E7. The await arm is final compiled-await revision `2e4fee1`. The combined delivery port `7b321a9` produces byte-identical linked artifacts from the same typed source under the final compiler. Both execution engines — native RV32 and Wasm — run on the actual PicoCalc P4. Native RV32 editor code executes directly on the P4 processor. Compilation also runs on the P4.

## 2. What Was Measured

The experiment has three layers. First, twenty-four frozen host semantic replays verify that all key revisions produce correct output. Thirteen of these replays compare the Editor application against its JavaScript reference. Five additional fixtures exercise timer and input order on real Wasm and emulated RV32 reactors; emulated RV32 applies only to these host-side fixtures, not to the physical P4 measurements described below.

Second, a physical short workflow runs the standard test — typing, file save/readback, simple Find, Markdown preview, discard, and cleanup — on the actual P4 hardware with three trials per engine per arm. Each trial compares two specific captured frames. Device firmware is built separately for the two engines. Wall time displayed to the app is fixed for screenshot consistency, but all timers and timeout decisions use the actual monotonic clock. The test directory name differs between engines by design, so only screenshots within an engine are compared.

Third, a Find query fixture delivers a specific search against a 65,536-byte buffer containing 851 CRLF lines of repeated text plus a final nine bytes `needlezzz`. Three query classes are tested: an early query matching at column 2 of line 1; a dense miss query (`text text z`) that exhausts all candidate positions; and a unique late query matching the needle at line 852, column 1. The measurement interval begins at delivering Enter in the query prompt and ends at producing a retained frame with the expected result. The elapsed clock includes scheduling; the separate Editor CPU clock sums only the Editor's execution segments; engine time includes reactor and SDK execution. The controlled delivery was necessary where normal kernel routing serializes requests; test-injected events are not physical keypresses. Search outcomes were verified on both physical engines before timings were accepted. Each query class has one physical trial per engine per arm. No confidence intervals or workload-wide speed claims can be drawn from such an exploratory sample. The code to reproduce is in PICOCALC-EG-QUAL/scripts.

## 3. Compiler Cost

Both compiler intervals are measured on the real P4. On the native RV32 target, median compilation time rose from 2,645,557 μs to 3,816,925 μs (+44.28%). On the Wasm target, it rose from 2,028,286 μs to 3,121,485 μs (+53.90%). Peak compiler heap followed the same pattern: 1,493,644 to 2,256,776 bytes (+51.09%) on RV32 and 1,545,892 to 2,263,468 bytes (+46.42%) on Wasm.

The first measured generated build missed the prespecified cold compile gate (`native_compile_within_10pct: False`). Its success or failure is separate from subsequent compiler experiments.

Separately measured rewrite-phase totals account for 896.5 ms of the 1,179.7 ms added to the native compile interval. The rewrite decomposes as: 440.8 ms reading input, 181.4 ms scanning for operations, 160.7 ms analyzing tasks, and 57.1 ms building rewritten text. The remaining approximately 283 ms falls in other compiler phases. The dominant added cost is reading and scanning the source, not control-flow analysis.

## 4. Output Artifact Size

The native RV32 module is delivered in a fixed-size envelope of 240,452 bytes in both arms. This identical envelope does not imply identical native instructions: the manual editor uses 21,922 native words while the await editor uses 22,292, a growth of 370 words. The G3 typed-await pass added 264 native words to its E6 control (21,922 to 22,186); G4 added 106 further (22,186 to 22,292). The Wasm module grew by 667 bytes, from 88,302 to 88,969 (+0.76%).

## 5. Runtime Performance

The full Editor workflow CPU time, measured across three physical P4 trials per arm, is closely matched. On RV32, medians are 35.03 ms (manual) and 34.80 ms (await), a difference of −0.66%. On Wasm, medians are 144.35 ms and 144.30 ms, a difference of −0.03%. The native workflow CPU passes the prespecified 10% gate (`native_cpu_within_10pct: True`).

## 6. Find Query Timing

The table below reports all measured values from the single physical trial per query class, engine, and arm. The elapsed clock includes host scheduling between segments. The Editor CPU clock sums only Editor execution segments.

| Engine | Query | Elapsed manual → await (ms) | Δ | CPU manual → await (ms) | Δ | Seg. | Settl. |
|--------|-------|-----------------------------|---------|-------------------------|---------|------|--------|
| rv32 | early | 4.52 → 4.09 | −9.52% | 4.50 → 4.06 | −9.83% | 1 → 1 | 0 → 0 |
| rv32 | late | 54.23 → 55.81 | +2.91% | 39.54 → 39.60 | +0.15% | 27 → 27 | 26 → 26 |
| rv32 | miss | 183.88 → 171.67 | −6.64% | 116.28 → 113.12 | −2.72% | 297 → 297 | 296 → 296 |
| wasm | early | 41.52 → 41.61 | +0.22% | 41.49 → 41.57 | +0.20% | 1 → 1 | 0 → 0 |
| wasm | late | 732.41 → 738.09 | +0.78% | 604.11 → 603.38 | −0.12% | 27 → 27 | 26 → 26 |
| wasm | miss | 1762.06 → 1656.60 | −5.98% | 1370.97 → 1277.17 | −6.84% | 297 → 297 | 296 → 296 |

The early hit completes in one Editor segment with zero settlements on both engines, confirming that a needle near offset zero returns before the first yield boundary. The late hit at line 852 produces 27 segments and 26 settlements. Line number alone does not predict search cost because the SDK can skip an entire line in a single seek operation. The miss query exhausts all candidate positions, producing 297 segments and 296 settlements — the most of any class. The difference between elapsed and CPU times reflects the scheduling boundaries: for example, the rv32 late hit spends 54.23 ms elapsed but only 39.54 ms in Editor CPU, with the remainder in scheduling across 26 settlements.

The equal segment and settlement counts between arms demonstrate that the two implementations take equal numbers of cooperative turns through the host for each query class. These counts do not establish that suspensions occur at identical byte offsets or that the implementations are equivalent across all possible workloads.

## 7. State Words

The await Editor declares 57 state words and the compiler generates 13 additional words, totaling 70. The manual Editor uses 71 state words. These counts cover the entire application, not just the search function. The 13 generated words include control metadata for both of the application's cooperative tasks. The title length, which previously occupied its own state word, was moved into an existing spare SDK buffer cell, contributing to the one-word net reduction.

## 8. Visual Equivalence

Both engines produce exactly one distinct screenshot hash per captured frame across all six physical runs (three manual, three await). The await Editor's visual output matches the manual Editor for every compared frame on both engines.

## 9. Limitations

Each Find query class has one physical trial per engine per arm. The workflow layer has three trials per arm and shows tight clustering, but the query layer does not support statistical inference. No hardware logic analyzer, key-to-pixel latency, or source-level instruction profile was collected. The physical sample timing is exploratory throughout.

## 10. Conclusion

The generated await transformation achieves equal cooperative turn counts, matching visual output, and no measurable runtime penalty on the integrated Editor workflow for both execution engines on the PicoCalc P4. The await arm uses one fewer application state word than the manual arm, while the native RV32 program grows by 370 words and the Wasm binary by 667 bytes. The cost is in compilation: +44–54% in time and +46–51% in peak memory, with the rewrite phase's input reading and operation scanning accounting for the majority of the added time. Because compilation runs on the P4 itself, this overhead is a material constraint. The first cold compile measurement missed the prespecified 10% gate. Whether this compile-time cost is acceptable depends on how frequently the editor is recompiled on-device versus shipped as a fixed artifact.

---

## Investigation Diary

1. **Prompt context.** The working directory is `/tmp/picocalc-eg-wave/empty`, not a git repository. The prompt supplies an experiment design for resumable text editor search, verified physical measurements from an implementation team, and a technical review with corrections to an initial report. The measurements reference git revisions `1357545` (manual), `2e4fee1` (await), and `7b321a9` (combined delivery port), prespecified gate labels G3 and G4 from PICOCALC-NATIVE-NEXT, and two execution engines on PicoCalc P4 hardware. All compilation and execution runs on the actual P4.

2. **Interpretation.** "Manual" corresponds to the hand-written continuation arm; "await" to the generated start/resume arm. The technical review corrected several interpretive errors in the initial report. This revision incorporates every correction.

3. **Inferred intent.** The project evaluates whether compiler-generated cooperative yields justify their compile-time cost for the PicoCalc Editor, where compilation occurs on the device itself. The report serves as both a technical record and pedagogical material for a compiler engineer joining the team.

4. **Corrections incorporated.** (a) Both compiler intervals are measured on the real P4, not a development host. The initial report incorrectly suggested shipping a fixed artifact compiled off-device. (b) Native RV32 editor code executes directly on the P4 processor; emulated RV32 applies only to separate host fixtures. The initial report did not distinguish these execution contexts. (c) The 13 Editor workflows are host semantic replays comparing the app to its JS reference; the physical short workflow is separate and compares two specific captured frames per trial, not every possible frame. (d) Equal segment and settlement counts demonstrate equal numbers of cooperative turns, not identical suspension byte offsets or universal equivalence. The initial report overclaimed that "generated yield points fire at exactly the same positions as the hand-written ones." (e) No 64-byte frame-size gate was established in the actual experiment. The initial report referenced a gate from the original design that was never adopted. (f) The 70-vs-71 state word counts cover the entire application. The 13 generated words include control metadata for both cooperative tasks. Title length moved into an existing spare SDK buffer cell. The initial report incorrectly attributed the one-word reduction to the generator eliminating a redundant variable. (g) The 240,452-byte native module envelope is a fixed slot. Identical envelopes cannot prove identical native instructions; the actual programs differ at 21,922 vs 22,292 native words. The initial report incorrectly treated identical envelope bytes as evidence of code-level identity. (h) Single paired query measurements are exploratory; no universal performance estimate or per-yield noise threshold can be extracted. The initial report made overly broad claims from single trials. (i) Only the native workflow CPU has a formal 10% gate. The initial report implied both engines had formal runtime gates. (j) The first measured cold compile missed its gate; this is separate from subsequent compiler experiments. The initial report framed it as "the single failing metric of the experiment" without noting its limited scope. (k) The compiler cost breakdown uses measured rewrite-phase components — 440.8 ms reading input, 181.4 ms scanning for operations, 160.7 ms analyzing tasks, 57.1 ms building rewritten text — rather than attributing the bulk of cost to live-variable analysis. The initial report speculated about liveness passes without data. (l) E1–E7 are E language tasks, not Find phases. The initial report mislabeled them. (m) Removed unsupported predictions about relative engine cost ratios.

5. **What worked.** The prespecified gates provide a clear pass/fail framework for the workflow layer. The screenshot hash comparison provides frame-level visual equivalence. The measured compiler cost breakdown identifies dominant components without speculation. Presenting the query timing as a single table with all six cells, both elapsed and CPU, makes the exploratory nature transparent.

6. **Tricky parts.** (a) The fixed 240,452-byte native envelope was the most consequential correction. The initial report's strongest claim ("the transformation adds compile-time work that leaves no measurable residue in the artifact") was wrong: native code grew by 370 words, hidden by the fixed envelope. (b) Distinguishing host semantic replays (24 frozen, 13 with JS reference, 5 fixture) from physical short workflow (P4 hardware, two frames per trial) required careful re-reading of the measurement notes. (c) The compiler cost breakdown required restating the initial report's entire narrative. The original attribution to live-variable analysis was replaced by measured components showing I/O and scanning dominate.

7. **Compiler cost breakdown detail.** The 1,179.7 ms of added native compile time decomposes as 896.5 ms in the rewrite phase and approximately 283 ms elsewhere. Within the rewrite: 440.8 ms (37% of total added) reading input, 181.4 ms (15%) scanning for operations, 160.7 ms (14%) analyzing tasks, 57.1 ms (5%) building rewritten text. Reading and scanning together account for 52% of the added compile time. This profile suggests optimization should target I/O throughput before algorithmic complexity of the transformation.

8. **Query timing observations.** The elapsed clock includes scheduling between Editor segments; the CPU clock excludes it. For the rv32 late hit, elapsed time is 54.23 ms but CPU is 39.54 ms, with approximately 14.7 ms consumed by 26 scheduling boundaries. For the wasm late hit, elapsed is 732.41 ms with CPU of 604.11 ms. The late hit at line 852 does not require scanning every preceding byte because the SDK can skip a line in a single seek. The miss query produces 296 settlements and spends the most time in scheduling boundaries. All timing figures are exploratory single-trial measurements.

9. **Native word growth.** G3 added 264 native words to E6 control (21,922 to 22,186). G4 added 106 further (22,186 to 22,292). The total growth of 370 native words represents the generated dispatch, frame management, and control metadata. This is distinct from the fixed 240,452-byte envelope, which serves as a delivery container and cannot be used to infer instruction-level equivalence.

10. **Visual equivalence scope.** The physical short workflow compares two specific captured frames per trial, not every possible frame. The screenshot hash uniqueness (one hash per shot across all six runs per engine) confirms those specific frames are identical between arms. This is a necessary but not sufficient condition for full visual equivalence.

11. **Predictions vs measurements.** The original design predicted GSR frames would be larger due to conservative live-variable capture — this prediction was not tested against a 64-byte gate (no such gate was established). The original design predicted yield counts would match — the measured segment and settlement counts match, confirming equal turns though not identical suspension offsets. The original design predicted runtime overhead would be measurable — workflow CPU differences are within noise (−0.66% and −0.03%), and query CPU differences in single trials range from −9.83% to +0.20%, all exploratory.

12. **Next steps.** (a) Collect additional trials for the query-layer measurements to support statistical comparison. (b) Determine whether the rewrite phase's input-reading cost (440.8 ms, the single largest component) can be reduced through caching or incremental compilation. (c) Evaluate the compile-time overhead in the context of on-device development iteration frequency.

13. **Review instructions for the implementation team.** Verify that revisions `1357545`, `2e4fee1`, and `7b321a9` are correctly identified as manual, await, and combined-port respectively. Confirm that the 65,536-byte fixture buffer is consistent across both engines and arms. If additional query trials are collected, update the report with them. The cold compile gate failure is noted as a separate event from subsequent compiler work. The E language tasks (E1–E7) are referenced only as workload coverage, not as Find phases.

14. **Technical detail: segment and settlement semantics.** A segment is one uninterrupted interval of Editor execution between entry (start or resume) and exit (yield or terminal return). A settlement is a host-acknowledged yield — the host received a yield, performed scheduling, and re-entered the guest. The early hit has 1 segment and 0 settlements: search returns a hit without yielding. Equal segment and settlement counts between arms mean the host observes the same number of cooperative turns for these query classes, confirming matched scheduling behavior without implying byte-level suspension equivalence.
